summaries.example: Imagine a town where some families cannot afford enough food, a safe place to live, or needed medical care. The town creates different kinds of help. It might provide food, offer a fair-paying job, or give money to someone who cannot work. The goal is to make sure everyone can reasonably reach the things needed for a decent life. People may still disagree about exactly what help the town should provide.
summaries.summary: A social minimum is the set of resources people need to live a minimally decent life in their society. A government or community can create policies so that everyone has reasonable access to those resources. Philosophers disagree about what belongs in the minimum. Some focus on happiness or satisfied wishes. Others focus on capabilities, or what people are really able to do and be. Still others focus on resources such as income and wealth. Each view has strengths and problems. Happiness can hide hardship when people become used to having very little. Money alone may not help everyone equally, because people have different health needs and abilities. The entry also asks whether the minimum should change with a society’s general wealth. Being unable to join ordinary social life may be a serious disadvantage even when a person has enough to survive. Arguments for a social minimum come from several theories of justice. Some say it increases overall well-being, protects people from desperate poverty, or supports equal citizenship. Critics worry about taxes, personal freedom, fairness, or people becoming dependent on assistance. The entry considers replies to these worries. It also examines whether help should depend on work or job-seeking. Such conditions might seem fair, but they can pressure people into unsafe jobs, harm dependents, or punish people who already face unfair opportunities. Finally, decisions about the minimum must be legitimate: people should be able to understand the reasons, question decisions, and take part in fair procedures.
key_ideas: A social minimum aims to make sure people can live at least a minimally decent life.
The needed resources may depend partly on the society people live in. What counts as enough for social participation can change as a society becomes richer.
Different ideas about justice give different reasons for supporting or questioning a social minimum.
Help does not always have to be handed out directly. A suitable, fair job may also give someone access to the needed resources.
Rules about work, taxes, and services should be made through fair and open decision-making.
A social minimum may protect freedom by giving people more choices and helping them avoid being controlled by others.
summaries.why_it_matters: The idea affects everyday questions about food, housing, health care, education, work, and participation in community life. It asks what people owe one another and how public rules should protect people from living in severe need. It also reminds us that helping everyone is not only about choosing a list of benefits. Communities must decide who receives help, under what conditions, and how much can fairly be provided. Those decisions can affect freedom, dignity, and people’s ability to speak and take part in society.

important_terms.definition: The basic resources and opportunities people need to live a decent life in their society.
A group of laws, services, and programs meant to help everyone reach the social minimum.
The real power to achieve important things, such as being healthy, learning, joining community life, or having self-respect.
The good feelings or satisfied wishes that some theories use to judge how well a person is doing.
A fair chance to reach needed help, which might come through money, services, or a suitable job.
The idea that some people may need different amounts of help to have the same real opportunities.

questions_to_think_about: What things does every person need for a decent life?
Should a person receive help even if they cannot work?
How can a community decide fairly what kinds of help to provide?
Could giving people help sometimes give them more freedom?
Should a rich society expect more than a poor society does?

summaries.example: Suppose a government wants to guarantee that every citizen can live above a minimally decent threshold. It could use tax revenue for cash assistance, health care, education, or housing support. It might instead rely partly on a fair job guarantee for people who can work, while directly providing resources to people who cannot. A utilitarian would ask whether the policy increases total welfare. A libertarian would ask whether taxation violates self-ownership or property rights. An egalitarian liberal might ask whether the worst-off are protected. A relational egalitarian would ask whether poverty leaves some citizens vulnerable to domination or unable to participate effectively in democracy.1
summaries.summary: The entry defines a social minimum as the resources needed for a person to lead a minimally decent life in their society, and a social minimum policy regime as institutions that secure reasonable access to it. “Reasonable access” is important because access might come through direct benefits, public services, or suitable employment rather than through an unconditional transfer in every case. The concept therefore does not settle the debate over conditionality. The first major issue is what should ultimately be secured. Welfarism focuses on happiness or desire-satisfaction, but adaptive preferences create a problem: people accustomed to deprivation may report satisfaction without having decent lives. The capability approach instead evaluates what people are actually able to do and be. It is more sensitive to differences in health and circumstances, but a fixed capability list may reflect a controversial conception of human flourishing. Resourcism seeks neutrality by emphasizing all-purpose means such as income and wealth, yet resources alone do not reveal what different people can achieve with them. An ecumenical capability approach attempts to identify widely important capabilities while respecting ethical and cultural diversity. It still faces the problems of deciding which capabilities belong on the list and how much provision is enough. The entry also distinguishes absolute from relative deprivation. Some requirements are basic everywhere, while social participation and self-respect may require more resources in wealthier societies. Several theories of justice can support a social minimum, though for different reasons. Utilitarian support depends on effects on total welfare and incentives. key_ideas: The social minimum is deliberately abstract: it leaves open both what a minimally decent life requires and how people should receive access to it.
Welfarism, the capability approach, and resourcism identify different objects of moral concern. Each avoids some problems while creating others.
An ecumenical capability approach tries to identify capabilities important across reasonable ethical outlooks while allowing sensitivity to cultural and social differences.

The minimum may have both absolute and relative aspects. Basic survival has an absolute dimension, while self-respect and social participation may require resources related to prevailing social standards.

Theories of justice support the social minimum for different reasons. Utilitarianism emphasizes aggregate welfare; egalitarian liberalism emphasizes protection for the least advantaged; relational egalitarianism emphasizes equal status, democratic participation, and freedom from domination.

Objections based on freedom, fairness, and legitimacy do not automatically defeat a social minimum, but they raise serious questions about taxation, conditionality, policy design, and decision-making.
summaries.why_it_matters: The social minimum is a central test for theories of justice because it connects abstract principles to urgent material conditions. It asks whether freedom is meaningful when poverty leaves people exposed to coercion by employers, landlords, or authorities; whether equality requires more than equal legal rights; and whether democratic participation is genuine when some citizens lack time, energy, or resources to use their political liberties. It also reveals that policy design matters morally. Decisions about cash or services, targeting or universal provision, and work conditions can alter people’s vulnerability and status. important_terms.definition: A bundle of resources sufficient, given a society’s circumstances, for a person to lead a minimally decent life.
A policy and institutional arrangement that gives all members a fair opportunity to reach the social minimum.
A person’s genuine opportunities to achieve valuable states and activities, rather than merely the resources they possess.
A person’s achieved states and activities, such as being nourished, healthy, socially connected, or able to participate.
The view that distribution should be assessed mainly by happiness or desire-satisfaction.
The view that income, wealth, or other means should be the primary objects of distribution, while trying to remain neutral about people’s plans.
The libertarian idea that people have strong rights over their bodies and abilities and therefore may not be forced to serve others’ purposes.
A view of equality concerned with power and status relations, including freedom from domination and effective participation as an equal citizen.

questions_to_think_about: Can a list of central capabilities be sufficiently neutral among reasonable views about the good life?
Should a social minimum be measured only by absolute resources, or partly by people’s position relative to their fellow citizens?
When, if ever, is it fair to make assistance conditional on work or job-seeking?
Does taxation for redistribution violate self-ownership, or can it distribute liberty more fairly?
What procedures would make decisions about health-care limits and other benefits legitimate even for people who disagree with the result?

summaries.example: Imagine a city where some students’ families cannot afford reliable meals, transport, internet access, or medical care. The city wants everyone to have a fair chance at a decent life. It might provide school meals and health services, give some families money, or offer adults suitable jobs. One person may say this is fair because it improves people’s well-being. Another may worry that taxes take away freedom. A third may say that help should depend on making a contribution. The city must consider these disagreements rather than assuming there is only one obvious answer.
summaries.summary: The social minimum is the collection of resources that people need to live a minimally decent life in their own society. A government can create a policy regime so that everyone has reasonable access to this level. “Reasonable access” is broader than simply giving everyone the same package. It might involve public services, cash, or a suitable job, as long as the arrangement is fair and actually helps people reach the minimum. A major philosophical question is what the minimum should secure. A welfare-based view looks at happiness or desire-satisfaction, but people who grow up with very little may lower their expectations and still report being satisfied. The capability approach looks instead at people’s real opportunities: whether they can be healthy, nourished, educated, socially connected, and able to direct their lives. It handles differences between people better than a simple income test, but critics worry that choosing a list of important capabilities may impose one view of a good life. A resource-based view tries to be more neutral by focusing on income, wealth, and other general means. Yet equal resources do not always produce equal opportunities because people have different needs. The entry also discusses relative deprivation. Some needs are absolute, such as avoiding serious hunger, but other needs depend on what is normal in a society. Being unable to participate in ordinary activities can damage self-respect even when a person is not starving. Theories such as utilitarianism, libertarianism, egalitarian liberalism, and relational egalitarianism give different reasons for supporting or limiting a social minimum. key_ideas: The social minimum is not one fixed amount of money. It is a set of resources and opportunities suited to the circumstances of a society.
Philosophers disagree about whether the goal should be happiness, capabilities, or resources.
People with the same income may have different opportunities because of health conditions, disability, or other circumstances.
A society may need both an absolute floor for basic survival and a relative standard for social participation and self-respect.
Some arguments support a social minimum because it can reduce poverty and help people participate as equal citizens. Other arguments worry about taxes, incentives, fairness, or dependence.
Work requirements may seem to encourage reciprocity, but they can pressure people into bad jobs and can harm dependents or people facing unfair background conditions.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic matters because it connects political philosophy to choices about taxes, health care, education, housing, income support, and employment. It also shows why “helping the poor” is not a simple idea. A policy can provide money yet fail to give someone a genuine opportunity because of illness, disability, unsafe work, or unfair social conditions. A social minimum may also strengthen democracy by giving people enough security to participate in public life and enough independence to resist domination in workplaces or families. At the same time, fair policy requires open reasons and procedures that allow people to challenge decisions.

important_terms.definition: The basic resources needed for a person to live a minimally decent life in the society where they live.
Policies and institutions that give people reasonable ways to reach the social minimum.
Real opportunities to do or be important things, such as being healthy, learning, or taking part in community life.
How well a person is doing, sometimes understood as happiness or getting what they want.
Money, property, services, or other tools people can use to pursue their own plans.
A person’s position compared with other people in the same society, especially when being far behind limits participation or self-respect.
Making benefits depend on an activity such as looking for work, training, or employment.

questions_to_think_about: What is the difference between having resources and having a real opportunity to use them?
Should the social minimum rise when most people in a society become richer?
Is it fair to require people who can work to search for a job before receiving assistance?
How might poverty reduce a person’s freedom, even if no one is directly ordering them around?
Who should help decide what services belong in the social minimum?
